Results: Diagnostic Candidate Generation

This section details the biophysical, thermodynamic, and specificity profiles of the primary and alternative diagnostic candidates generated by the pipeline.

By running three distinct geographical filtering scenarios, we track how database constraints shape the molecular properties, degeneracy, and safety of the resulting primer and probe sets:

  1. Indonesia Only (indo-only): Tailored strictly to local Indonesian strains.
  2. Southeast Asia Only (sea-only): Tailored to regional Southeast Asian strains.
  3. All-Partial Database (all-partial): Incorporates local focal strains (Indonesia) alongside global contextual sequences.

1. Biophysical and Thermodynamic Profiles of Candidate Sets

To ensure high-efficiency PCR amplification, candidate sets were screened for optimal melting temperatures (\(T_m\)), GC content, and secondary structure thermodynamics (hairpin and dimer free energy, \(\Delta G\)).

Below are the profiles of the top three designed primer/probe sets for each scenario, formatted as molecular cards for readability:

  • Indonesia Only Candidates
  • Southeast Asia Only Candidates
  • All-Partial Database Candidates

2. Secondary Structure Stability (Thermodynamic Safety)

To prevent self-priming, hairpin loops, and primer-dimer complexes, the engine evaluated each set’s free energy (\(\Delta G\)):

  • Hairpin Veto Threshold (\(\Delta G \le -9.0\) kcal/mol): Hairpins with strong folding energies can block polymerase extension. All M1 design candidates (Indo-only and SEA-only) showed a hairpin \(\Delta G\) of -4.21 kcal/mol, and M2 candidates (All-partial) showed -2.81 kcal/mol, which are well within the safe range (\(>-9.0\) kcal/mol).
  • Cross-Dimer Veto Threshold (\(\Delta G \le -12.0\) kcal/mol): Primer-dimers compete with target amplification. The cross-dimerization energies range from -7.59 to -9.30 kcal/mol, showing that stable primer dimers are thermodynamically unfavorable under standard PCR cycling conditions.

3. IUPAC Degeneracy and Target Coverage Trade-offs

IUPAC degenerate bases (such as R for A/G, Y for C/T, K for G/T) are added to primer sequences to ensure the assay can bind to templates containing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) circulating in the population:

  • Regional Designs (Indo-Only & SEA-Only):
    • Designed in the conserved 187–352 bp M1 region, the primers require a degeneracy multiplier of 16 to achieve \(>99.5\%\) coverage of local sequences. This low degeneracy count is ideal because high degeneracy can dilute the concentration of the active primer species in the PCR mix.
  • Global Design (All-Partial):
    • Because global background sequences introduce high entropy, the M2 target primers require a degeneracy multiplier of 16 for Rank 1 and 2, but Rank 3 requires a higher degeneracy of 32 (on the forward primer) to accommodate global variation, illustrating how database size and geographic filters dictate degeneracy demands.

4. Specificity Verification and BLAST Veto Filtering

All generated candidates were filtered through the NCBI BLAST+ Specificity Verification Engine (Module 09) using local databases (human_db for host DNA and virus_db for non-target respiratory viruses):

  • The 3’ End Veto Filter: If a candidate pair matches any non-target respiratory pathogen or human sequence with zero mismatches in the last 8 nucleotides at the 3’ end, the set is vetoed (FAIL).
  • In-Silico Specificity Scores:
    • Virus Specificity: All top candidates achieved a perfect 100.0 score with 0 off-target viral alignments, confirming no cross-reactivity with common respiratory pathogens (including SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Adenovirus, and Rhinovirus).
    • Human Specificity: The candidates showed high specificity, with human safety scores ranging from 73.6 to 93.9 (where scores above 70 indicate negligible off-target binding).
  • Veto Action Statistics:
    • Indo-Only: Out of 100 raw candidates, 12 sets were vetoed due to critical 3’ end cross-reactivity with the human genome.
    • All-Partial: 22 candidate sets were vetoed due to human genomic cross-reactivity, reflecting the higher sequence complexity of the 3’ M2 region.
